To kneel means to go down on one or both knees and rest your body's weight on them, rather than standing or sitting. When you kneel, your knee (or knees) touch the ground or floor, and you are supporting yourself on that part of your leg just below the thigh.

Think of it this way: your leg has three main parts — the thigh (upper leg), the knee (the joint in the middle), and the lower leg. When you stand, your feet are on the ground. When you kneel, you fold your legs and bring your knee down so that it becomes the part touching the ground.

Imagine a person standing upright. To kneel, they:

  1. Bend one or both legs at the knee.
  2. Lower the body until the knee or knees rest on the ground.
  3. The upper body can remain upright, or it can lean forward.

You can kneel on one knee (think of a person proposing marriage — one knee on the ground, one foot still planted) or on both knees (think of someone praying at a church pew, both knees on the floor).

Kneel is an irregular verb. Here are all its forms:

  • Base form: kneel (I kneel)
  • Present participle: kneeling (I am kneeling)
  • Past tense: knelt (I knelt) — this is the most common past form
  • Past tense (alternative): kneeled (I kneeled) — also correct, but less common
  • Third person singular: kneels (She kneels)

The verb "kneel" appears in many different situations. Understanding those situations will make its meaning click more deeply.

1. Prayer and worship
This is perhaps the most universal use. People kneel before God, before an altar, or at a place of worship to show humility and devotion. The physical act of lowering yourself — making yourself smaller — symbolizes that you consider the divine to be far greater than you.

"She knelt beside her bed every night to pray."

2. Submission and surrender
Throughout history, kneeling before a ruler, a king, or a person in authority was a way of showing that you submit to their power. A soldier who surrenders may kneel. A subject receiving an honor from a king kneels before him. The body language carries a clear message: I am beneath you; you are above me.

"The knight knelt before the queen to be honored."

3. Respect and mourning
People kneel to pay respect — at a grave, at a memorial, or in a moment of silence. The gesture communicates deep reverence and emotional sincerity that simply standing cannot express.

"The team knelt on the field for a moment of silence."

4. Protest
In modern times, kneeling has taken on a powerful new meaning as a form of peaceful protest. The idea is to refuse to stand in a moment when standing signals agreement or national pride — instead, kneeling signals silent, dignified objection. The most famous example of this is athletes kneeling during national anthems to protest racial injustice.

"The footballer knelt during the anthem to protest discrimination."

5. Practical, everyday tasks
People also kneel simply because the task requires it — tying a child's shoes, gardening, fixing something under a table, comforting a small child at their level, or searching under a bed.

"He knelt down to tie her shoelaces."
"She knelt in the garden to pull out the weeds."

You'll often see "kneel" used with directional words:

  • Kneel down — the act of going from standing to a kneeling position. (She knelt down beside him.)
  • Kneel before / in front of — to kneel in the presence of someone or something, usually to show respect or submission. (He knelt before the altar.)
  • Remain kneeling — to stay in the kneeling position. (The crowd remained kneeling in silence.)

Sometimes "kneel" is used in a non-literal, symbolic sense to mean to submit, to give in, to show complete humility or defeat.

"The nation refused to kneel to oppression."

Here, no one is physically getting on their knees. The word is used to mean: they refused to surrender, they refused to bow down. This figurative use is powerful because it draws on all the connotations of submission and powerlessness that kneeling physically represents.
How It Differs From Similar Words

It helps to understand what kneeling is not, so you don't confuse it with related actions.

  • Bow — to bend the head or upper body forward as a sign of respect, while remaining on your feet. You bow standing up. Kneeling involves going all the way down to your knees.
  • Crouch — to bend your legs and lower your body close to the ground, but balancing on your feet (not your knees). You crouch to hide or to pick something up quickly; you'd stand back up easily. Kneeling specifically means the knee touches the surface.
  • Prostrate — to lie flat on the ground, face down, in a gesture of total submission or worship. This is more extreme than kneeling. Prostrating is the whole body on the floor; kneeling is just the knees.
  • Sit — when you sit, your bottom is on a surface (a chair, the floor). When you kneel, your knees are on the surface and your bottom is either raised or resting on your heels.

Kneeling carries emotional weight. It is rarely a neutral, casual act. When a character in a story kneels, it almost always signals something significant — reverence, surrender, grief, love, or defiance (as in the protest context). Writers and filmmakers use kneeling deliberately because the body language is deeply expressive.

Kneeling on one knee vs. both knees also carries different implications in culture:

  • One knee: Romantic proposals, a knight being honored, a respectful but not fully submissive gesture.
  • Both knees: Deep prayer, complete submission, extreme reverence, or intense grief.

Kneeling can be uncomfortable. Hard surfaces make kneeling painful after a while. This is why people use kneeling pads in gardens, why churches have padded kneelers, and why soldiers are trained to adopt it as a stable but temporary position. This physical discomfort also adds to its symbolic power — it is a gesture that costs you something, which is precisely what makes it meaningful.

To kneel is to lower your body so that one or both knees rest on the ground, rather than standing on your feet. It is an action that physically expresses humility, respect, devotion, submission, love, or grief — depending on the context. It is used literally (prayer, proposals, gardening) and figuratively (refusing to kneel = refusing to submit). Its past tense is most commonly knelt, and the ongoing action is kneeling.
